title: Developer Debug Playbook: Partial Streams & Tool Replay
content:
TL;DR:
This playbook describes pragmatic debugging and developer tooling patterns to make partial/interruptible streaming responses and tool-call replays reproducible, observable, and easy to test locally. It proposes a small set of API primitives, SDK helpers, telemetry events, and a local test harness so engineers can debug live production incidents and reproduce them deterministically in a dev environment.

Background / problem statement:
- Hosted streaming responses are often partial (progressive output frames, synthetic checkpoints, tool call fragments). When issues occur (truncated output, missed tool callbacks, inconsistent structured output), engineers need to reproduce the exact sequence of frames and tool interactions.
- Current debugging workflow is: reproduce high-level request, observe final output, and rely on logs. That is slow for intermittent partial failures and hard to trace tool-handshake races or client-side replays.
- We need a low-friction developer flow for capturing a streaming session, replaying it deterministically locally, and iterating on SDK/handler fixes.

Goals:
- Define lightweight session capture and replay primitives that preserve ordering and causal relationships between frames and tool calls.
- Add SDK helpers to record and replay streams with minimal API changes for customers and internal engineers.
- Standardize telemetry events to make post-mortem reconstruction of partial sessions straightforward.
- Provide a local dev harness (CLI + small server) that can inject captured sessions into SDKs and server-side tool adapters for repeatable tests.

Non-goals:
- Full formal transactional guarantees for tool calls (beyond idempotency tokens and clear replay semantics).
- Large changes to public API surface; prefer additive flags and optional headers.

Key user personas and scenarios:
1) Backend engineer investigating truncated JSON in a streaming chat response: needs to reconstruct the exact sequence of partial frames, the point a tool call was triggered, and the client-side resume attempt.
2) SDK engineer fixing an off-by-one frame ordering bug: wants to replay a captured session with deterministic timing to validate fixes.
3) Solutions engineer demonstrating robust retries to a customer: wants an easy way to simulate flaky networks and partial tool failures.

Proposed primitives and contracts:
- Session Capture (opt-in header): X-RW-Capture: true. When set, the platform will emit a capture bundle reference id at session end (or on explicit close). Capture bundles contain an ordered list of frames with timestamps, frame types (text, json-blob, tool-invoke, tool-response, checkpoint), tool call ids, and idempotency tokens.
- Fragment identifiers: each emitted frame includes fragment_id (string) and seq (int). Clients can use these to assert ordering and request resends for missing seqs.
- Commit markers: a small frame type "commit" marks a logically complete response snapshot that SDKs can use for reconciliation.
- Replay header: X-RW-Replay: <bundle-id> instructs the server or local harness to replay the exact captured frame sequence.
- Tool call idempotency: tool_invocations include tooling_id and idempotency_key. During replay the platform guarantees the tool_invocation frame is emitted but the downstream tool adapter will receive the invocation with an X-RW-Replay header so the adapter can decide to simulate failure or return cached results.

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing helpers):
- captureStream(session): Promise<bundleId> — simple helper that toggles capture and returns the reference id.
- replayStream(bundleId, options): runs the captured session locally or against a staging endpoint. Options: speedFactor (float), dropFrames (list of seq ints), injectDelay(ms).
- onFrame({fragment_id, seq, type, payload}) callback signature standardized across languages.
- snapshotCheckpoint(): emits a local commit marker and waits for server ack when using capture mode.
- built-in CLI tool (rw-capture) to fetch bundle content, visualize frames (ascii + json), and run replay scenarios with configurable network jitter.

Telemetry and logging schema (required fields added to existing event model):
- event: frame_emitted — attrs: session_id, fragment_id, seq, type, elapsed_ms, capture_bundle_id (optional)
- event: frame_ack — attrs: session_id, fragment_id, seq, client_ack (bool)
- event: tool_invoke_sent — attrs: tool_id, tool_call_id, idempotency_key, session_id, fragment_id
- event: tool_result_received — attrs: tool_call_id, status, latency_ms, session_id
- event: replay_started / replay_finished — attrs: bundle_id, initiated_by, run_id
All telemetry events should be queryable by capture_bundle_id and session_id to ease rebuilding the timeline.

Local dev harness (minimum viable):
- rw-capture CLI: fetch --bundle <id> -> writes JSONL file; visualize --bundle <file> -> colorized frames; replay --bundle <file> [--speed 0.5] [--drop 12,13] -> replays to local SDK endpoint.
- small replay server > receives replay frames and forwards them to a connected SDK using standard streaming transport (websocket/http2). It can optionally proxy tool-invoke frames to a local tool-adapter (with flags to simulate timeouts/failures).
- example docker-compose with a simple echo tool-adapter demonstrating idempotency semantics.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Internal SRE/solutions engineers can capture and replay sessions for 90% of production incidents that involve partial streams within 48 hours of capture availability.
- Post-deploy mean time to reproduce (MTTR) for streaming partial-output incidents reduces by 40% measured across Q2 pilot teams.
- SDKs expose capture/replay helpers in node/python/go SDKs with consistent API surface and minimal churn.
- Telemetry allows constructing ordered frame timelines for captured bundles via a single query by bundle id.

Compatibility and rollout strategy:
- Phase 1 (internal pilot, 6 weeks): implement capture bundle generation on staging, add SDK helpers in Node + Python, ship rw-capture CLI, and test with internal teams (SRE, SDK, Solutions).
- Phase 2 (beta customers, 8 weeks): enable capture opt-in for selected tenants, provide access to captured bundles via console and CLI, collect feedback.
- Phase 3 (public opt-in): enable capture for all hosted-api customers via account flag and console toggle; add replay endpoints in dedicated environments.

Security and privacy considerations:
- Captures may contain PII and customer data. Bundle storage must respect tenant isolation, TTL defaults (30 days), and encryption at rest.
- Capture bundles access should be restricted via RBAC and audit-logged. CLI access requires short-lived tokens.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: volume of capture data increases storage and cost. Mitigation: default sampling rate 0.1% for production, opt-in on a per-tenant basis, TTL pruning, and ability to redact payloads via redact rules before storage.
- Risk: replay may cause side effects on downstream tools. Mitigation: include replay header, and require explicit allow-listing for replays to call live downstreams (default: local simulated adapters).

Open questions / discussion items:
- Should captures store full binary payloads for embeddings and attachments, or references only? (tradeoff: fidelity vs storage).
- Is a server-side replay service (multi-tenant) needed, or is local CLI-first sufficient for initial rollout?
- UX: what level of visualization (timeline vs state diffs) helps engineers fastest?

Next steps and immediate action items:
- Owner (Evan): prototype capture bundle format and wire minimal frame_emitted telemetry. ETA: 2 weeks.
- SDK (Liam): spike Node SDK helpers for capture/replay with demo app. ETA: 3 weeks.
- SRE (Maya): build rw-capture CLI stub and local replay server; integrate with internal incident runbook. ETA: 4 weeks.
- Security (Rohit): draft capture storage retention and RBAC model for review. ETA: 1 week.

Appendix: example captured frames (JSONL, simplified)
{"fragment_id": "f-9a1e", "seq": 1, "type": "text", "payload": "Hello"}
{"fragment_id": "f-9a1e", "seq": 2, "type": "tool-invoke", "tool_call_id": "t-42", "payload": {"name": "search", "args": {"q": "weather"}}, "idempotency_key": "abc-123"}
{"fragment_id": "f-9a1e", "seq": 3, "type": "tool-response", "tool_call_id": "t-42", "payload": {"results": [...]} }
{"fragment_id": "f-9a1e", "seq": 4, "type": "commit", "payload": {"summary": "final"}}

Contacts / owners: Evan Chen (product) — evan.chen@redwood.ai; Maya Ortiz (SRE) — maya.ortiz@redwood.ai; Liam Park (SDK) — liam.park@redwood.ai; Rohit Gupta (security) — rohit.gupta@redwood.ai

Notes: this is intentionally opinionated and pragmatic — the goal is to unblock incident reproduction and SDK fixes quickly, not to fully standardize all streaming protocols. Feedback welcome; will iterate after pilot.
